text: Dana's requisition has approval. Before it becomes a purchase order, every line still needs an answer to a question nobody in Self Service Procurement asks out loud: which account actually absorbs this cost?

A distribution is the part of the line that specifies the accounting - how much goes to which charge account. Dana's fifty bearings have a single distribution covering the full amount, though a requisition could split cost across multiple accounts if departments were sharing a purchase.

The charge account isn't typed in. It defaults from rules set up back in Enterprise Structures, drawing on the requester's default expense account, the cost center, and the item category. Since the bearing is categorized as an MRO expense item, it defaults to a maintenance expense account on Dana's plant cost center.

If LTV has encumbrance accounting enabled, approving the requisition can reserve funds against the budget immediately - a requisition encumbrance - even before any purchase order exists. That protects against over-committing a budget before a buyer is even involved.

This charge account isn't cosmetic. It's the exact account that gets debited later and the one you'll trace all the way into the General Ledger in chapter five. Up next, lesson nine: processing Dana's approved requisition into Marcus's purchase order.
